kedsomhed.explanation: "En kedsomhed" means "boredom". For the thing that is boring, use "kedelig" (boring) instead: "Filmen er kedelig" (The film is boring).

kemi.explanation: "Kemi" means "chemistry". As a school subject, Danish uses it with no article: "Vi har kemi på torsdag" (We have chemistry on Thursday).

kemisk.explanation: "Kemisk" means "chemical". To say clothes are taken to be cleaned without water, use "kemisk rensning" (dry cleaning): "Jeg afleverer jakken til kemisk rensning" (I am dropping the jacket off for dry cleaning).

kendskab.explanation: "Et kendskab" means "knowledge", as in being familiar with a place or a subject. To say you know something well, use "til" (of) after it: "Jeg har godt kendskab til byen" (I have good knowledge of the city). For facts you have learned, use "viden" (knowledge) instead: "Hun har stor viden om historie" (She has great knowledge of history).

kendt.explanation: "Kendt" means "famous". To say what someone is known for, it also means "known", with "for" (for) after it: "Hun er kendt for sin musik" (She is known for her music).

kikærter.explanation: "Kikærter" means "chickpeas". The word is plural. To talk about one, use "en kikært" (a chickpea).

kina.explanation: "Kina" means "China". Spell it with a "K" and no "h". To say you travel there, use "til" (to): "Jeg rejser til Kina" (I am traveling to China).

kinesisk.explanation: "Kinesisk" means "Chinese". Danish does not capitalize it, unlike English: "kinesisk mad" (Chinese food). For the language, use it alone: "Jeg taler kinesisk" (I speak Chinese).

klam.explanation: "Klam" means "clammy". When something feels cold and sticky, use it: "en klam hånd" (a clammy hand). When you find something disgusting, it also means "gross": "Det er så klamt" (That is so gross).

klar.explanation: "Klar" means "clear". When someone is prepared, it also means "ready": "Er du klar?" (Are you ready?) To answer "of course", say "Det er klart" (Of course). Do not mix it up with "færdig" (finished): "Jeg er færdig" (I am finished).

klassisk.explanation: "Klassisk" means "classic". To call something a lasting favorite, put it before the noun: "en klassisk bil" (a classic car). When you talk about music, it also means "classical": "klassisk musik" (classical music).

klatring.explanation: "En klatring" means "climbing". It is the noun for the verb "at klatre" (to climb).

klimaforandring.explanation: "En klimaforandring" means "a climate change". It is built from "klima" (climate) and "en forandring" (a change). To talk about the global problem, use the plural "klimaforandringer": "Vi taler om klimaforandringer" (We are talking about climate changes).

klimapolitik.explanation: "En klimapolitik" means "a climate policy". It is built from "klima" (climate) and "en politik" (a policy). To name one party's, put the party before it: "partiets klimapolitik" (the party's climate policy).

klodset.explanation: "Klodset" means "clumsy". To say someone put words badly, use it for what they said: "Det var en klodset bemærkning" (That was a clumsy remark).

klog.explanation: "Klog" means "wise". For a person who thinks well, it also means "smart": "Hun er meget klog for sin alder" (She is very smart for her age). To say something was a mistake, say "Det var ikke særlig klogt" (That was not very smart).

klokken.explanation: "Klokken" means "o'clock". Literally, it means "the clock". To tell the time, say "Klokken er tre" (It is three o'clock). To say when something happens, say "Vi mødes klokken otte" (We meet at eight o'clock). In writing, it is shortened to "kl."

klokken er fem.explanation: "Klokken er fem" means "It's five o'clock". To ask the time, say "Hvad er klokken?" (What time is it?) and the answer starts with "klokken er". Danish counts half hours toward the next hour: "halv tre" (literally "half three") means half past two, as in "Klokken er halv tre" (It is half past two).

knapt.explanation: "Knapt" means "barely". To say something hardly happened at all, add "nok" (enough): "Han har knapt nok sovet" (He has hardly slept at all).

knust.explanation: "Knust" means "heartbroken". For a person who is very sad, use it: "Hun er knust efter nyheden" (She is heartbroken after the news). For things, it means "smashed": "Glasset var knust" (The glass was smashed).

knækbrød.explanation: "Et knækbrød" means "a crispbread". It comes from "at knække" (to snap), because it snaps when you break it.

kobber.explanation: "Kobber" means "copper". For a wire made of copper, add "tråd" (wire): "Jeg har købt en rulle kobbertråd" (I bought a roll of copper wire).

kogt.explanation: "Kogt" means "boiled". It comes from the verb "at koge" (to boil). Do not mix it up with "stegt" (fried): "en stegt kartoffel" (a fried potato).

kokain.explanation: "Kokain" means "cocaine". Spell it with a "k" in place of both "c" letters: "kokain".
